note: One machine-readable source for topic defaults, the security profile, and the client settings that invariant 1 depends on. Partition defaults and session.timeout.ms are MEASURED (S4, S5, 2026-09-20) on a 3-broker 1 GB-heap cluster in a 7.4 GiB Docker VM on a Windows laptop: they are lower bounds, not cluster limits. Values marked TODO await ADR-004 or a Linux re-measurement.
apply_order_note: A topic-creation tool MUST apply the class configs and THEN the profile overrides. Applying only the class configs is safe by default because they carry the production durability values.

must_not_hardcode.$comment: NORMATIVE, see README.md 3.7. Every value below is read from this file - loaded at startup or generated into constants by the build - and never restated as a literal in packages/ or deploy/. min.insync.replicas is the reason: it is a TOPIC-level config, so a topic created without it inherits the broker default of 1, acks=all is satisfied by one replica, the receiver still ACKs, and the next broker loss drops an acknowledged message. Invariant 1 false with every setting apparently correct. A copied literal in one of five places is how that HIGH finding returns.
must_not_hardcode.acceptance: devops-engineer and platform-engineer each keep a test asserting the component's effective configuration equals the value here. session.timeout.ms and the partition defaults will be re-measured on Linux; a duplicated literal is a place that re-measurement silently fails to reach.

lite.approval: Human-approved profile exception to invariant 1's durability promise, 2026-09-21 (ADR-002 D14). The invariant itself is NOT edited. See README.md 3.8.
lite.warning: RF=1 with min.insync.replicas=1 cannot guarantee RPO=0 for acknowledged messages. Development and accepted-risk small sites only; the runtime must log this at startup. This is the ONLY place the durability floor may be lowered, and it is deliberately explicit rather than inherited.
lite.warning_acceptance: MANDATORY and testable: emitted at WARN level in the structured log by any component started against a lite-profile cluster, on by default, with no flag to suppress it. A test asserts it is emitted under lite and not otherwise - a warning nobody can prove fires is the same as no warning.

durability_floor.$comment: Invariant 1. These two settings are repeated in every class below on purpose: min.insync.replicas is a TOPIC-level config, so a topic created without it inherits the broker default of 1, and acks=all is then satisfied by a single replica. A broker loss at that moment loses an acknowledged message. unclean.leader.election.enable is likewise topic-level and must be pinned per topic, not only cluster-wide.

raw.partitions_source: MEASURED (S4, ADR-002 D5): 1,000 channels at 3 partitions per topic = 12,009 partitions, healthy on 3 brokers with 1 GB heap. At the former default of 12 the cluster was lost at about 425-450 channels, failing the 500-channel threshold. Override per channel where throughput needs more.
raw.max.message.bytes_source: DECIDED 2026-09-26, kept at 1,048,576; NOT an envelope control. Kafka checks max.message.bytes against the record BATCH AFTER COMPRESSION, and raw is compression.type=producer (receivers send lz4). So no value here can make the broker refuse a payload over the envelope's 1,000,000-byte inline limit: a compressible 5 MB HL7 payload passes as a small lz4 batch. The gap above 1,000,000 is therefore not 48,576 bytes but unbounded for compressible data. Lowering to the envelope-derived bound (conservative upper bound 1,019,105 = 61 batch header + 36 worst-case record varints and attributes + 256 key + 1,000,000 payload + 32 x 10 header-length varints + 32 x 64 header names + 16,384 header values) would refuse only uncompressed or incompressible oversize records, and would read as a guarantee it does not give. The controls that do hold: WRITE on raw only for the receiver principal (README 3.4); receivers refuse input over 1,000,000 bytes (channel-spec 3.2.2); a worker that cannot dead-letter halts the partition with TB_DLQ_UNWRITABLE (envelope 2.3.2). Real fix: claim-check.

out.partitions: match the raw topic of the same channel
out.constraint: MUST equal the raw partition count when the channel declares per-key ordering, otherwise the key-to-partition mapping differs and per-key order breaks (invariant 5). The runtime refuses to start on a mismatch.

retry.partitions: match the raw topic of the same channel

dlq.partitions_source: keyed by tb-msg-id, low volume, read by humans. S4 suggests 1 would do for retry and dlq, but that was not tested, so it is not adopted.

reply.partitions_source: matches the channel default (S4). Set 1.2: overridden ONLY by channel-spec spec.source.reply.partitions (1-64), never by spec.partitions, because the reply topic is sized by receiver processes, not throughput: each process must hold at least one partition (README 3.3.1). It need not match raw - replies are routed to an explicit partition, not by key hash. Sync-reply channels add a fifth topic, so the sharing trigger's channels x 4 x partitions projection understates them: add reply.partitions per sync channel.
reply.created_when: Only for a channel whose spec has source.reply (set 1.2). An async channel has no reply topic.

events.partitions_source: ADR-001 planning value, STILL UNMEASURED: no Phase 0 spike exercised the archive path under load. TODO(Phase 1): confirm against the measured event rate.

audit.retention_note: Decided 2026-10-06 (set 1.8; README 2.1; ADR-004 R2, R6, R7): this topic is a 30-day transport buffer, not the system of record. Audit records are kept in the ClickHouse audit_log table, with retention set by the operator through TB_ARCHIVE_AUDIT_TTL_DAYS (default 2190 days, range 1-36500), applied by the archiver migrate step. The default is conservative, not a compliance determination. Bootstrap creates this topic.

security.note: A deployment that implements only the blocks above gets a plaintext, unauthenticated, unauthorized cluster carrying PHI. Transport security and authorization are part of this contract, not a separate hardening guide. Values marked TODO are deployment-specific; the requirement is not.

broker.client_listeners: SASL_SSL, or SSL with mTLS. PLAINTEXT is permitted only on a loopback-bound lite listener that no non-local client can reach.
broker.inter.broker.listener.name: an internal listener using SASL_SSL or mTLS
broker.authorizer.class.name: org.apache.kafka.metadata.authorizer.StandardAuthorizer
broker.super.users: Set 1.4.1: the broker's own identity (inter-broker and controller links), the topic-creation job and an operator admin principal. A one-shot user-provisioning identity, where the deployment has one, is NOT a super user: it holds only ALTER on CLUSTER (what AlterUserScramCredentials needs; the same grant authorises CreateAcls, so its key is super-user-grade). NEVER a data-plane component, NEVER the control plane's channel publisher (it holds only its control_plane grants), NEVER User:ANONYMOUS. Principal names are deployment-specific; the lite stack's are in engine-kafka/v0 README section 6 rule 3.

clients.sasl.mechanism: SCRAM-SHA-512 or OAUTHBEARER. Never PLAIN on a listener without TLS.
clients.ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm_no: Leave hostname verification enabled. Disabling it is the single most common way a TLS Kafka deployment silently accepts a man-in-the-middle.
clients.credentials: Set 1.3 (ADR-008): every data-plane process reads one contracts/engine-kafka/v0 document named by TB_ENGINE_KAFKA_FILE (bootstrap servers, protocol, secretRef names), and resolves the secretRefs from local files under TB_SECRETS_DIR at start. The principal names are deployment-specific and ADR-004's. Never in a channel spec, a Compose file or an image; the Compose lite stack generates per-component SCRAM users at `up`.
clients.plaintext: Loopback brokers only (127.0.0.0/8, [::1], localhost), enforced by every data-plane role, with no opt-out flag or profile. A container network is not loopback. engine-kafka/v0 section 4.

encryption_at_rest.note: Kafka has no built-in encryption at rest. Volume-level encryption protects a lost disk, a decommissioned disk and a shared snapshot; it does NOT protect against a compromised broker, an over-broad ACL or an unaudited Kafka UI. See README.md 3.5.
encryption_at_rest.broker_data_dirs: encrypted volumes (LUKS, cloud disk encryption, or an encrypted storage class)
encryption_at_rest.claim_check_bucket: bucket-default encryption on (SSE-KMS, SSE-S3 or the MinIO equivalent). Largest single PHI store in the system: whole payloads.
encryption_at_rest.archive_volumes: ClickHouse and PostgreSQL on encrypted volumes
encryption_at_rest.backups: encrypted, same rules as the source volume
encryption_at_rest.application_level_encryption: NOT required in v0 and not designed here; it is key management, which is ADR-004 plus a human decision
encryption_at_rest.key_custody: TODO(ADR-004): cloud-managed versus customer-managed KMS keys. The requirement that encryption be on is not a TODO.

acls.model: Deny by default, least privilege per component, granted on the topic prefix <env>.<channel>. so one channel's compromise does not read another's traffic.
acls.grammar: Set 1.4. Each role string is parsed by the lite topic-bootstrap (deploy/compose/topic-bootstrap/bootstrap_topics.py parse_grants), so keep its form: a first sentence of '<OPS> on <targets>' clauses separated by ';', then only 'Set 1.2, sync-reply channels only: ...' or 'No <OP> on <kind>, so ...' sentences. A target without '*' is a LITERAL resource; a target ending '*' is PREFIXED on everything before the '*', so every prefix here ends at a '.' or '-' delimiter; 'group ' names a consumer group; 'the cluster' is the cluster resource. READ and WRITE imply DESCRIBE in Kafka's authorizer, so DESCRIBE is not listed separately.
acls.reconciled_with_code: Set 1.4, 2026-09-29: every grant below is one a role's code path uses, found by reading packages/tributary-runtime (worker.py, channels.py, topics.py), packages/tributary-loaders/*/main.py and packages/tributary-receivers. No role holds a grant no code uses, except the receiver's _tb.<env>.channels READ, granted ahead of its invariant-3 migration (README 3.4.1).
acls.receiver: WRITE, DESCRIBE on <env>.<channel>.raw; IDEMPOTENT_WRITE on the cluster; READ on _tb.<env>.channels; READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.channels.*. Set 1.2, sync-reply channels only: READ on <env>.<channel>.reply and READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.replier. No WRITE on reply, so a receiver cannot forge an answer
acls.pipeline_worker: READ on <env>.<channel>.raw; WRITE on <env>.<channel>.out.*, .dlq; WRITE on _tb.<env>.events; READ on _tb.<env>.channels; READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.pipeline and tb.<env>.<channel>.pipeline.shadow-*; READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.channels.*. Set 1.2, sync-reply channels only: WRITE on <env>.<channel>.reply
acls.pipeline_worker_transactional: Set 1.4. Only for a channel with pipeline.transactional true, in addition to pipeline_worker: WRITE on the TRANSACTIONAL_ID resource PREFIXED tb.<env>.<channel>.pipeline. (the clients.transactional_stage_producer transactional.id template). Kept out of the pipeline_worker string because the lite parser has no transactional-id target and the demo channel is not transactional; without the grant the worker fails at init_transactions with TRANSACTIONAL_ID_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, before consuming (fail closed).
acls.loader: READ on <env>.<channel>.out.<dest>; WRITE on <env>.<channel>.dlq; WRITE on _tb.<env>.events; READ on _tb.<env>.channels; READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.loader.<dest>; READ on group tb.<env>.<channel>.channels.*
acls.loader_retry_topic: Set 1.4, NOT GRANTED in v0: retry.policy retry-topic is refused by the schema and no code reads or writes <env>.<channel>.retry. When it lifts (channel-spec README 4.1.1), the loader gains READ, WRITE on <env>.<channel>.retry and consumes it in its OWN destination group tb.<env>.<channel>.loader.<dest>, filtering on tb-destination. A channel-wide retry group is forbidden: topics README 3.4.1.
acls.archiver: READ on _tb.<env>.events, _tb.<env>.audit; READ on group tb.<env>.archiver
acls.archiver_audit_note: Set 1.8 part 2 (W3-1b; ADR-004 R7): the events archiver also consumes _tb.<env>.audit into ClickHouse audit_log (contracts/audit/v0), LITERAL, in the same group. No WRITE: the archiver can never forge an audit record. Takes effect when W3-30 part 2 subscribes; granting it earlier is harmless.
acls.archiver_note: Set 1.8: group grant LITERAL (was PREFIXED tb.<env>.archiver*, which broke rule 2 of README 3.4.1 and would also have matched the groups of a channel named 'archiver'). Group name as built in W3-2a (tributary.archiver.config.archiver_group, per archive-engineer's report; the architect has not read the code). Still owed: confirm the archiver touches no other topic, group or cluster resource (W3-23 style exact-grant test).
acls.reprocessor: READ, WRITE, DESCRIBE on <env>.<channel>.raw; IDEMPOTENT_WRITE on the cluster; DESCRIBE on group tb.<env>.reprocessor
acls.reprocessor_note: Set 1.8 (W3-29; wave-3.md 2.6 H8). Granted per channel: replay and reprocess target only their source channel, so the topic grant is LITERAL <env>.<channel>.raw, never PREFIXED <env>. (which would also grant WRITE on out, dlq and reply). READ fetches the original payload. The consumer uses assign() and never joins or commits, but librdkafka requires a group.id and still sends FindCoordinator for it, so the LITERAL platform group tb.<env>.reprocessor gets DESCRIBE only, no READ (measured by archive-engineer on a deny-by-default broker, lead-relayed; the architect has not run it). Its producer enforces the receivers' 1,000,000-byte input limit. Human sign-off folds into ADR-004 H7.
acls.lag_reader: DESCRIBE on <env>.*, _tb.<env>.events; DESCRIBE on group tb.<env>.*
acls.lag_reader_note: Set 1.8 (W3-29; wave-3.md 2.5 H4). Used by KEDA and the lag exporter only. DESCRIBE on topics PREFIXED <env>. and LITERAL _tb.<env>.events, DESCRIBE on groups PREFIXED tb.<env>.: enough to read end offsets and committed offsets, never a payload. No READ, no WRITE, no cluster grant. UNVERIFIED until the W3-23-style test shows KEDA reading lag under this role alone.
acls.control_plane: WRITE on _tb.<env>.channels and _tb.<env>.audit; DESCRIBE on the cluster
acls.forbidden: No data-plane component gets cluster-wide WRITE, DELETE or ALTER, and none gets WRITE on _tb.<env>.channels — a compromised worker must not be able to deploy a channel spec.
acls.open_question: The complete role model, credential rotation and key management are ADR-004 plus a human decision. This block is the minimum shape that the config contract must state, not the finished model.

receiver_producer.linger.ms_source: TODO set from the S2 ACK-latency-versus-throughput curve
receiver_producer.compression.type_source: assumption, unmeasured: cheaper CPU than zstd for small text records

worker_consumer.isolation.level: read_committed on topics written by a transactional stage
worker_consumer.max.poll.interval.ms: at least the slowest destination timeout plus backoff
worker_consumer.session.timeout.ms_source: MEASURED (S5 and S4, ADR-002 D5.1). This is the recovery-time floor for an ordered channel: a killed worker's partitions cannot move until its session expires. S5 measured 10.01 s and 11.32 s takeover at a 10 s setting; S4 measured 43.8 s static-member removal at the 45 s Kafka default, from a different harness. 10-15 s is the recommended band; shorter raises the risk of spurious rebalances on a loaded or GC-pausing worker.
worker_consumer.commit_every_source: MEASURED (S5): committing every 50 records instead of every 1 gave 4.9x throughput (151 -> 733 msg/s) for a replay window of 50 instead of 1. Invariant 4 requires loader idempotency on tb-msg-id anyway, so a window of 1 buys little. 50 is the value that was measured; the surrounding curve was not, so it is a measured point rather than an optimum.
worker_consumer.commit_every_note: This is the REPLAY WINDOW: after an unclean worker death, up to this many records are redelivered (S5 measured 12 replayed at commit_every=20). At-least-once permits that and an idempotent loader absorbs it. A destination declaring idempotency.technique 'none' in its channel spec has no such absorber, so up to 50 visible duplicates at that destination is the consequence - lower it per destination, or accept it in the justification note the channel spec already requires.
worker_consumer.commit_every_scope: Deployment-level in v0. Deliberately NOT a channel-spec field: it is an operational tuning knob rather than channel semantics, and there is no evidence yet about per-destination variation. Revisit when there is.

reply_consumer.$comment: Set 1.2 (W2-8). The receiver's consumer of <env>.<channel>.reply in synchronous reply mode, one per receiver process, in group tb.<env>.<channel>.replier. Kafka's assignment IS the lease on a reply partition; there is no coordinator (invariant 3). README 3.3.1.
reply_consumer.commits: never. A reply older than this process's pending map is useless, so there is nothing to resume from
reply_consumer.isolation.level_source: the reply producer is not transactional: sync reply is refused on transactional channels (channel-spec README 3.2.6)
reply_consumer.group.instance.id: unique PER PROCESS (not per pod or receiver instance): a duplicate fences a live process out of the group
reply_consumer.group.instance.id_format: <instance>-p<pid>. Set 1.7: --instance is REQUIRED when source.reply is present (no default; the pid is 1 in every container, so a default collides across replicas). Deployment rule: unique per receiver replica of a channel per environment; Helm templates it from the pod name (downward API metadata.name or StatefulSet ordinal), Compose sets it per service. A fenced process (librdkafka _FATAL) is not ready and exits non-zero
reply_consumer.session.timeout.ms_source: same measured value as worker_consumer (S5, S4). Here it bounds how long a killed process's reply partition stays unusable; it stalls no other process
reply_consumer.read_from_here: Set 1.7. These are the reply consumer's own typed values (int ms; auto.offset.reset and isolation.level strings). The receiver reads them from clients.reply_consumer, NOT from clients.worker_consumer and not as literals: equal today, but a Linux re-measurement of the worker's session timeout must not move the replier's silently, nor the reverse (README 3.7)
reply_consumer.advertise_rule: A process advertises partition p in tb-reply-partition only after it holds p AND its consumer has an established fetch position on p. With auto.offset.reset=latest and no committed offsets, a reply written between assignment and the offset reset would otherwise be skipped
reply_consumer.not_ready_rule: A process holding no reply partition, or whose reply consumer is disconnected, answers sync requests AR / REPLY_UNAVAILABLE before publishing and fails its readiness probe

partition_budget.$comment: MEASURED (S4, ADR-002 D4). Projected total partitions = channels x 4 x partitions, plus reply.partitions for each sync-reply channel (set 1.2: its fifth topic is sized separately). Applies per tenant partition group, since a share group may not cross a tenant boundary.
partition_budget.share_new_channels_at_partitions_basis: measured: highest count tested healthy (1,000 channels at 3 partitions per topic, 1 GB heap, 3 brokers)
partition_budget.believed_fatal_at_partitions_basis: ONE failure in ONE run at a computed count of about 21,000. Nothing was tested between 12,000 and 21,000, so the cliff could be anywhere in that range. Do not scale with heap: the 2 GB runs were inconclusive.

platform_groups.$comment: Set 1.8. Environment-wide groups with no channel segment. The archiver reads _tb.<env>.events for every channel, so 'archiver' moved out of roles, where the pattern implied a per-channel group nothing builds.

consumer_groups.roles_note: replier (set 1.2) = the receivers' reply-consumer group in synchronous reply mode, on this engine's cluster (clients.reply_consumer). receiver (set 1.1) = a kafka source's group on the EXTERNAL cluster it reads; README 3.6 added it in set 1.1 and this list omitted it until set 1.2

spec_reader.$comment: Set 1.4. The _tb.<env>.channels reader every data-plane process builds (tributary.runtime.channels.open_spec_source). It uses assign(), never subscribe(), and never commits, but librdkafka still looks up the coordinator for a configured group.id, which needs READ (implying DESCRIBE) on the group: without it the worker logged GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED (error_code 30) at start on the lite stack. One group per process, so readers never share offsets or partitions.
spec_reader.acl: READ on group PREFIXED tb.<env>.<channel>.channels. (trailing '.' delimiter), for receiver, pipeline_worker and loader
